title.narrative: Technical Assistance to increase Budget Transparency (Phase II)

description.narrative: Contract related to: Technical Assistance to increase Budget Transparency (Phase II) - The National Rectangular Strategy IV (RS IV) 2019-2023 has at its core a comprehensive good governance reform programme. In line with the RS IV, as well as with the objectives of the Government Public Financial Management Reform Programme, improvement in governance is one of the most important factors for inclusive and sustainable growth in Cambodia.Improvements in economic governance will therefore also help to foster better results in all the other priorities of the MIP. Building on the previous MIP, the implementation of the Public Financial Management (PFM) Reform Program will allow to enhance fiscal discipline, further increase domestic resource mobilisation and improve policy-based budgeting and allocation of financial resources for an improved service delivery to citizens, including in education and skills.The proposed Action is for continued strategic partnership with the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) MEF through support to the implementation of the national PFM Reform Programme (PFMRP) in the transition from its 3rd stage (CAP3) 2017-2020 and the Consolidated Action Plan 3+2 (CAP3+2) 2021-2022, which is focused on the establishment of budget-policy linkages, to its 4th stage (future CAP4 2023-2027) that will aim at performance accountability (performance-informed budgeting). The proposed Action contributes to the MIP Priority Area 3 (Good Governance) and to its Specific Objective 1 to improve efficiency, transparency and accountability in management of public funds to improve public service delivery. Good governance underpins the two other priority areas of Green growth and decent jobs and Education and skills development; without a better functioning public financial management, the potential for a transformative impact of all interventions will be at risk. The Action¿s overall objective is to promote sustainable, inclusive and climate neutral economic recovery post-Covid-19. The specific objectives are (1) Enhanced budget credibility; (2) Enhanced financial accountability and transparency; and (3) Strengthened efficient budget-policy linkages, including on Climate Change and Gender (4) Capacity Building for PFM and service delivery. The Action will focus in particular on domestic resource mobilisation, revenue management (administration and policy), budget comprehensiveness and transparency, public investment management, public procurement, digitalisation through the financial management information systems (FMIS), accounting and reporting, and national statistics.It is proposed to continue using the budget support modality together with a strong policy dialogue and complementary measures through direct technical assistance. The Action will also introduce Twinning projects for the first time in Cambodia to support capacity building and inter-institutional cooperation.This Action is expected to contribute to the achievement of SDGs 16 (Peace, justice and strong institutions) and 17 (Partnerships), and indirectly to most other SDGs such as SDGs 3 and 4 on Good health and Quality education which require substantial quality investment in people and infrastructure but also to SDG 1 (No poverty), SDG 8 (Decent work and economic growth), SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 5 (Gender equality), through green and gender budgeting.

title.narrative: Improved Public Investment Management regulatory framework

description.narrative: The last Public Investment Management Assessment (PIMA) was conducted in Cambodia in 2018 (report published in 2019), before the climate module was added. The PIMA report provided a useful diagnostic that served to inform the development of the Public Investment Management System Reform Strategy (PIMSRS) adopted by Government in October 2019. The document aims at integrating all public investment (domestically and externally financed, PublicPrivate PartnershipsPPP, national and subnational) into the Public Investment Plan (PIP), and at harmonising management regulations. The Strategy is to be operationalised through the overarching SubDecree on Public Investment Management (No.41, approved in March 2020) and a series of SubDecrees and Prakas currently under development, which will include the detailed Standard Operating Procedures for the project cycle of each investment category: externallyfinanced (already approved in March 2020), PPP, domesticallyfinanced, subnational domestic, asset swap and commercial loans. The reform gives MEF the role of a `gatekeeper to oversee all investment projects (above a certain threshold) via a Public Investment Committee (PIC, formally established in December 2021). The PIC will ensure integration of planning and budgeting through a twostage prioritization process, first through PIP projects, which will be completed before the start of annual budget discussions, and second through a prebudgeting phase where PIP projects will be further prioritized for budget financing.Whereas the PIMSRS 20192025 and SubDecree No. 41 on PIM (2020) mention the objective of environmental sustainability and resilience to climate change in general terms and require environmental impact assessments for medium and large investment projects, they do not integrate the broader climate change perspective and all the aspects that can be improved in that direction at the planning, coordination, project appraisal and selection, budgeting, and risk management stages. The MEF, however, is committed to conducting a ClimatePIMA in 2022 (with IMF in the lead), and to gradually upgrade its legal and regulatory framework after that, starting with the overarching SubDecree No. 41 on PIM (2020) and then with the Standard Operating Procedures for external, national, subnational and PPP financing to integrate the climate change perspective taking into account CPIMA recommendations. The Standard Operating Procedures for the key regulatory framework to operationalise the overarching SubDecree No.41 on PIM, and in particular to set the detailed rules for project planning, appraisal and selection, procurement (when relevant) and monitoring.

comment.narrative: The Standard Operating Procedures SOPs for externally funded investment projects are in place since 2020 but not reflecting strongly the climate change perspective the SOPs for domestically funded investment projects subnational investment projects publicprivate partnerships are still being developed as of February 2022.
The Standard Operating Procedures SOPs for external national subnational and PPP financing are revised to enhance the Climate Change perspective in line with revised SubDecree No.41

title.narrative: Degree of implementation of the The Strategic Capacity Development Plan 20212025

description.narrative: Capacity development, institutional strengthening and structural reorganisation have been identified as an important component of the PFMRP. The key objective is to ensure that capacity is being built in alignment with the emergence of new processes resulting from platform development. Without such an alignment MEF would not be able to sustain change and the whole reform process could collapse. To reach that objective, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance relies on the Economic Finance Institute (EFI), responsible for conducting training needs analyses and for developing and delivering a wide range of training programmes. The first Strategic Capacity Development Plan covered the period 20172020. It aimed at introducing a comprehensive training system, with EFI providing training of trainers and technical advice to line ministries and to other training institutions. The programme reached out to some 9,500 trainees identified in central government (i.e. line ministries and their provincial departments, but not districts/municipalities) through the delivery of around 80 courses. In spite of budget and capacity constraints, about 80 courses were delivered annually. The staff of EFI was also increased by 18 staff in 2017, to 124 teaching staff in total. EFI has finalised the current SCDP 20212025, based on a training needs analysis conducted in 2019 with inputs from line ministries and provincial departments. The current SCDP has been developed based on international standards (more participatory, based on the competency framework, with institutional capacity to be included and behaviour change) and with external support. The SCDP covers both the central and subnational levels.

comment.narrative: The Strategic Capacity Development Plans aim is to strengthen institutional resources to support changes in public financerelated performance. However progress in this part was slower than planned due to resources being focused on drafting the new public financial system law and subdecrees 81 and 82 which will pave the way for implementation of performanceinformed budgeting ahead. The development of a framework for the performance monitoring has not progressed as planned yet.
The Capacity Development Plan in the Framework of Public Financial Management Reform Program is implemented

description.narrative: Capacity development, institutional strengthening and structural reorganisation have been identified as an important component of the PFMRP. The key objective is to ensure that capacity is being built in alignment with the emergence of new processes resulting from platform development. Without such an alignment MEF would not be able to sustain change and the whole reform process could collapse. To reach that objective, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance relies on the Economic Finance Institute (EFI), responsible for conducting training needs analyses and for developing and delivering a wide range of training programmes. The first Strategic Capacity Development Plan covered the period 20172020. It aimed at introducing a comprehensive training system, with EFI providing training of trainers and technical advice to line ministries and to other training institutions. The programme reached out to some 9,500 trainees identified in central government (i.e. line ministries and their provincial departments, but not districts/municipalities) through the delivery of around 80 courses. In spite of budget and capacity constraints, about 80 courses were delivered annually. The staff of EFI was also increased by 18 staff in 2017, to 124 teaching staff in total. EFI has finalised the current SCDP 20212025, based on a training needs analysis conducted in 2019 with inputs from line ministries and provincial departments. The current SCDP has been developed based on international standards (more participatory, based on the competency framework, with institutional capacity to be included and behaviour change) and with external support. The SCDP covers both the central and subnational levels.

comment.narrative: The Strategic Capacity Development Plans aim is to strengthen institutional resources to support changes in public financerelated performance. However progress in this part was slower than planned due to resources being focused on drafting the new public financial system law and subdecrees 81 and 82 which will pave the way for implementation of performanceinformed budgeting ahead. The development of a framework for the performance monitoring has not progressed as planned yet.
The Capacity Development Plan in the Framework of Public Financial Management Reform Program is implemented

title.narrative: Conduct and implementation of PIMA recommendations

description.narrative: Conduct and implementation of PIMA recommendations

comment.narrative: Overall Cambodia has made significant progress in strengthening its public investment management framework since 2019. Both on institutional strength and effectiveness asmeasured by the PIMA framework progress was booked. Three of the 15 PIMA institutions were upgraded fiscal rules and targets alternative infrastructure financing and project selection and one reduced national and sectoral planning on institutional strength. The latter was due to tightening of the scoring framework since the publication of the PIMA handbook. Beneath this modest improvement some 12 of the 45 dimensions of the institutional framework showed real improvement and only one decreased in score. Effectiveness improved for 4 institutions fiscal targets and rules multiyear budgeting project selection and procurement. Effectiveness still lags behind institutional development considerably but the improvements noted by the mission are certainly more than just paper based. Interestingly and as evidence of the overall positive trend the measure of macro level public investment efficiency increased with more than 10 percent since the 2019 PIMA. Behind the overall results successful reforms were identified but also areas for continued improvement. In terms of success for example a debt ceiling was introduced to guide fiscal policy the quality of the mediumterm fiscal framework MTFF improved capital expenditure ceilings were imposed in the budget preparation process the regulatory framework for appraisal and selection was strengthened through a government subdecree and new standard operating procedures a new PPP law was enacted and a supporting general department established in the Ministry of Economy and Finance MEF and a legal framework was established for a new review and monitoring framework for large investment projects through a newly established Public Investment Committee PIC. Continued weaknesses however are evident in coordination of public investment between levels of government mediumterm capital budgeting and transparency the maintenance framework procurement and project implementation project and portfolio monitoring and monitoring of public assets. A crosscutting issues that requires attention is the IT development for PIM processes where fragmentation duplication and remaining gaps are concerns.

By the end of the programme the objective is for the Government of Cambodia to implement PIMA recommendations to a medium degree and therefore to show concrete improvements in the strengthening of Public Financial Management

title.narrative: Scoring of Cambodia in Climate Public Financial Management Assessment (CPIMA)

description.narrative: Public Investment Management Assessment (PIMA) is a comprehensive framework to assess infrastructure governance practices for countries at all levels of economic development. Specifically, PIMA evaluates 15 institutions involved in the three key stages of the public investment cycle: Planning of sustainable investment across the public sector; Allocation of investment to the right sectors and projects; Implementation of investments projects to deliver productive and durable public assets.Each institution is assessed on both institutional strength (the organization, policies, rules and procedures on paper) and effectiveness (the degree to which the intended purpose is being achieved in practice or there is a clear useful impact).PIMA also covers a qualitative assessment of three crosscutting factors that often impact the overall effectiveness of public investment management: (1) the legal and regulatory framework, (2) staff capacity, and (3) IT systems.

comment.narrative: There are 5 areas in the CPIMA assessment C1. Climateaware planning C2. Coordination between entities C3. Projection appraisal and selection C4. Budgeting and portfolio management C5. Risk management each with 3 dimensions. The CPIMA was completed for the first time in March 2023 hence there was no implementation of its recommendations yet. 2 out of 15 indicators are assessed as High 3 out of 15 as Medium and 10 out of 15 as Low.
The PIMA recommendations are implemented at least to some extent. it will be unlikely that a second PIMA is conducted in the next 34 years.

title.narrative: Strengthening, diversification and increase of Domestic Revenue Mobilisation (DRM) (2)

description.narrative: Introduction of a Personal Income Tax (PIT), including Capital Gains Tax (CGT), is envisaged in the Revenue Mobilisation Strategy (RMS) 20192023, which aims at broadening of the revenue base through revised tax and nontax policies and modernizing revenue administration, with a focus on improving taxpayer services and increasing voluntary compliance. Expanding the tax base is also to compensate for future stagnation of customs revenue (currently half domestic revenue) expected from ASEAN integration and contribute to create fiscal space to finance propoor government policies expenditures (education, health, social protection) and public infrastructures.This indicator aims at supporting governments plans to introduce a coherent PIT with simple rules, easy for the General Department of Taxation (GDT) to implement and for taxpayers to understand and to comply with. A feasibility study for PIT introduction was launched in 2016 with EU/SIDA support. Besides broadening the tax base, the PIT will also contribute to tax equity with progressive taxes, which will benefit the social welfare that primarily benefits poor people, women and children.In 2019, the authorities decided to postpone the introduction of the PIT due to lack of time to prepare the legal framework and to train district tax offices. The Covid19 crisis further delayed PIT implementation, including the CGT which was to be implemented as of 2022, and is now postponed to 2024. This indicator is expected to provide an incentive for government to keep CGT and PIT introduction on track, along with complementary TA to be provided under this programme.

comment.narrative: Capital Gains Tax is not in place
The Capital Gains Tax is implemented

title.narrative: Status of quality of performance indicators in CAP4 and PFMRP Annual Monitoring Reports

description.narrative: PFMRP monitoring is coordinated by the General Secretariat of PFM Reform Steering Committee (GSC). The GSC also provides support to lineministries and MEF general departments, both in the implementation and monitoring and evaluation of the implementation of the PFMRP. GSC is directed by a Secretary General assisted by six Deputy Secretary Generals in six divisions, including the Administration, Finance, and Monitoring and Evaluation Division (AFMED). The key roles and responsibilities of GSC include:oDesign policies, strategies, and consolidated action plan (CAP). GSC also supported implementing agencies within MEF and LMs as they prepare their own action plans (GDAPs and MAPs) under this framework.oPreparation of quarterly and annual PFMRP progress reports which raise issues and propose solutions to PFM Reform Committee and PFM Steering Committee or PFM Technical Working Group during quarterly and annual meetings.oFormulation of the budget to support the whole PFMRP. oCoordination with other crosscutting reform programs, including Public Administrative Reform and D&D Reform, to ensure these three reform programs are synchronized. oDissemination of the PFMRP to all stakeholders to ensure the awareness of reform program.
